pharm: Oral fumarate prodrug rapidly hydrolyzed to the active metabolite monomethyl fumarate (MMF), which activates the Nrf2 antioxidant-response pathway; immunomodulatory effect in MS.

summary: Dimethyl fumarate is an oral delayed-release capsule for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis in adults (clinically isolated syndrome, relapsing-remitting disease, and active secondary progressive disease). It is a prodrug converted to monomethyl fumarate (MMF), which activates the Nrf2 oxidative-stress pathway. Dosing starts at 120 mg twice daily for 7 days then increases to 240 mg twice daily. Key safety concerns include progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), a serious JC-virus brain infection that has been fatal and is associated with prolonged lymphopenia; lymphopenia and other serious opportunistic infections (including herpes zoster); anaphylaxis and angioedema; liver injury; and very common flushing and GI effects. Obtain a CBC including lymphocyte count and liver tests before starting and monitor during therapy.
indications: Treatment of relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis (MS) in adults, including clinically isolated syndrome, relapsing-remitting disease, and active secondary progressive disease

dosage.n: Swallow capsules whole and intact; do not crush, chew, or sprinkle on food

dosage.d: May temporarily reduce to 120 mg twice a day
dosage.n: Resume 240 mg twice daily within 4 weeks; consider discontinuing if unable to return to maintenance

admin: Swallow delayed-release capsules whole and intact - do not crush, chew, or sprinkle the contents on food
May be taken with or without food
Taking with food reduces the incidence of flushing; alternatively, non-enteric coated aspirin up to 325 mg taken 30 minutes before the dose may reduce flushing
Obtain a CBC including lymphocyte count before initiation
Obtain serum aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase, and total bilirubin before starting treatment
moa: The exact mechanism in MS is unknown. Dimethyl fumarate (DMF) is rapidly hydrolyzed by esterases to its active metabolite monomethyl fumarate (MMF). DMF and MMF activate the Nuclear factor (erythroid-derived 2)-like 2 (Nrf2) pathway, which is involved in the cellular response to oxidative stress; MMF is also a nicotinic acid receptor agonist in vitro. These actions are thought to underlie anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective effects.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to dimethyl fumarate or any excipient (reactions have included anaphylaxis and angioedema)
relative: Pre-existing lymphopenia or low absolute lymphocyte count (increased PML/infection risk)
Serious active infection (consider withholding until resolved)
Pre-existing significant hepatic impairment/abnormal liver tests
monitor: CBC with lymphocyte count (baseline, at 6 months, then every 6-12 months)
Liver tests: AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase, total bilirubin (baseline and as clinically indicated)
Signs/symptoms of PML, herpes zoster, and other opportunistic infections

preg: There are no adequate human data. In animals, adverse effects on offspring survival, growth, sexual maturation, and neurobehavioral function occurred when DMF was given during pregnancy and lactation at clinically relevant doses; a no-effect dose for developmental toxicity was not identified in rats. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: There are no data on the presence of DMF or MMF in human milk, or on effects on the breastfed infant or milk production. Consider the developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding alongside the mother's clinical need for the drug and any potential adverse effects on the infant.
renal: No dosage adjustment is necessary. No dedicated studies in renal impairment were conducted, but renal impairment would not be expected to affect MMF exposure (exhalation of CO2 is the primary elimination route).
hepatic: No dosage adjustment is necessary and hepatic impairment is not expected to affect MMF exposure; however, clinically significant drug-induced liver injury (transaminases >=3x ULN with total bilirubin >2x ULN) has been reported. Obtain liver tests at baseline and during treatment as clinically indicated, and discontinue if significant drug-induced liver injury is suspected.

moderate: Other immunosuppressive or immunomodulatory drugs - additive risk of lymphopenia, PML, and serious infections (use caution; not formally studied)
minor: No interactions identified with CYP enzymes or P-glycoprotein in vitro
Interferon beta-1a and glatiramer acetate - no effect on MMF pharmacokinetics
Aspirin (given ~30 min before) - does not alter MMF pharmacokinetics
Combined oral contraceptive (norelgestromin/ethinyl estradiol) - no relevant effect on contraceptive exposure
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; taking with food reduces flushing (~25% lower incidence) and a high-fat meal lowers MMF Cmax by ~40% without changing AUC.
interactions.alcohol: No specific drug-alcohol interaction described in labeling.
interactions.diagnostics: Can cause lymphopenia (decreased lymphocyte counts), elevated hepatic transaminases, transient eosinophilia, and proteinuria (albumin in urine).

serious: Liver injury (elevated transaminases; rare clinically significant injury)
Herpes zoster and other serious opportunistic infections
emergency: PML - progressive weakness on one side, limb clumsiness, vision disturbance, or changes in thinking/memory/orientation; withhold drug and evaluate immediately
Anaphylaxis / angioedema - difficulty breathing, urticaria, swelling of throat and tongue (discontinue and do not restart)
Serious opportunistic infection (e.g., disseminated herpes zoster, CNS infection)

monitoring: CBC including lymphocyte count: before initiation, after 6 months, then every 6-12 months; consider interruption if lymphocytes <0.5 x 10^9/L persist >6 months
Liver tests (AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase, total bilirubin): before initiation and during treatment as clinically indicated
Vigilance for PML, especially with prolonged lymphopenia; MRI/CSF JCV evaluation if suspected
Signs and symptoms of herpes zoster and other infections
Flushing and GI tolerability, particularly in the first month
counsel: Take one capsule twice a day, swallowed whole - do not crush, chew, or open them
Flushing (warmth, redness, itching) and stomach upset are common, especially in the first month, and usually ease over time; taking with food or aspirin 30 minutes before can help flushing
Get the blood tests your doctor orders (lymphocytes and liver tests) before and during treatment
Report new weakness on one side, clumsiness, vision changes, or confusion/memory changes right away - these can signal a serious brain infection (PML)
Seek emergency care for trouble breathing, hives, or swelling of the throat or tongue (allergic reaction)
Report shingles, fever, or other signs of infection, and tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning pregnancy
pk: MMF detectable rapidly after oral dosing; therapeutic onset in MS not defined
Median Tmax of MMF ~2-2.5 hours (delayed to ~5.5 h with high-fat meal)
Terminal half-life of MMF ~1 hour; no MMF circulating at 24 hours in most people
Dosed twice daily; no accumulation with multiple doses
Store at 15 C to 30 C; protect capsules from light
pearls: PML (progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy) is the most feared risk - a JC-virus brain infection that has been fatal; risk linked to prolonged lymphopenia (counts <0.8 x 10^9/L for >6 months). Withhold at first sign or symptom and evaluate
Check CBC with lymphocytes at baseline, 6 months, then every 6-12 months; interrupt if lymphocytes <0.5 x 10^9/L persist >6 months
Flushing and GI upset are very common early (month 1) and usually self-limited; food or non-enteric aspirin (<=325 mg) 30 minutes before dosing reduces flushing
Standard dosing: 120 mg BID for 7 days, then 240 mg BID (480 mg/day total)
Anaphylaxis/angioedema can occur after the first dose or at any time - discontinue and do not restart
Monitor liver tests; clinically significant drug-induced liver injury has been reported
missed: If a dose is missed, do not take a double dose to make up for it. Take the next dose at the regularly scheduled time and continue the usual twice-daily schedule.
overdose: Reported overdose symptoms were consistent with the known adverse-effect profile. There is no known antidote and no established way to enhance elimination of the drug. Manage with symptomatic, supportive treatment as clinically indicated.
